The World Today · ABC listen

US to restore trading relations with China

Broadcast Wednesday, 20 September 2000 · Reporter: Tom O'Byrne

← Full The World Today episode — Wednesday, 20 September 2000

COMPERE: Well, it's been a warm welcome from President Clinton for the Senate vote extending permanent normal trade relations to Beijing. Senior American business leaders have also applauded the Senate's decision, saying it ushers in a new phase of US/China commercial ties. As the Congressional vote has shown, much of the talk these days focuses on the economic revolution which is now well and truly under way in the People's Republic.

But in the back rooms favoured by the Beijing leadership, apparently another revolution is taking shape, one with ramifications every bit as far?reaching as anything that economic changes have promised.

Our China correspondent, Tom O'Byrne, reports that next month's Communist Party anniversary may be the last before a wholesale and publicly peaceful leadership transition takes place.

TOM O'BYRNE: For much of its 51 year hold on power, the critics have been forecasting the end of the Communist Party in China, the general view being that a party that came to power through revolution would be forced from power in much the same way. Yet despite half a century of social, economic and political upheaval and its popular support at rock bottom, the party's hold on power has never been in dispute.

China watcher and author of 16 books on the subject, Laurence Brahm [phonetic].

LAURENCE BRAHM: I think you're going to have a one-party system for a very, very long time. What you will see growing though is greater transparency in that party. You're going to probably have a gradual introduction of election and direct election within the party. You already have that happening. You have the grass roots elections in the township areas. Now you have that being introduced into urban areas. You're eventually going to have that introduced into government departments, and I think what you will create is a system of accountability and transparency that still is in the one party system.

TOM O'BYRNE: It's now also a party undergoing a generational transfer of power. As with much in China's Byzantine politics, the manoeuvring in this dynastic shift is well advanced. Some well-sourced academics suggest Jiang Zemin is keen to maintain his power base beyond the next party congress in 2002, despite pledging along with half the ageing Polit Bureau to step down.

President Jiang is also General Secretary of the Communist Party and Chair of the Central Military Commission, in effect the boss of all three key power structures in China. While all the others are expected to honour the deal, the 73 year old Jiang remains a wild card. His anointed successor, Hoo Jing Tau [phonetic], will probably take over as Party Secretary, but there's talk that like Dung Xao Ping [phonetic] did before him, Jiang will stay on in charge of the all-powerful military post for some time to come.

Laurence Brahm says Jiang has been preparing the party for transition.

LAURENCE BRAHM: He's telling party congress, "You've got to change too. We've got to stay a step ahead, we can't be behind, otherwise we're not going to be in a position of power." There's in turn also a move on right now, not just at the top level but at all levels, to try and bring in younger [indistinct], younger people into the bureaucracy.

TOM O'BYRNE: There's always been a talk of a gerontocracy in place in China. Is there such a fundamental shift that we're seeing an end to that or at least a phasing out of that?

LAURENCE BRAHM: I don't think we're seeing an end of it, but I think we're seeing the beginning of a phasing out, but I think you're going to see a much younger, much more open, much more in tune with the west leadership coming into position, not just at the top level but at the medium, middle level and lower level as well.

TOM O'BYRNE: The next few years, say China watchers, will prove critical in the transition process. A healthy economy and trouble-free economic and social reform bodes well for the party's reformist technocrats maintaining the ascendancy over the military. What's not so clear is the effect on the leadership if things go the other way.

This is Tom O'Byrne in Beijing for The World Today.
